summary: Module 4 REFLECT (Critical Review, Senior Engineer phase). The five failure categories are now a lens, not a checklist: SECURITY = the IDOR is the #1 AI failure because ownership verification is business logic, not a pattern -- I closed it by embedding require_owner_or_admin in the build prompt and PROVING it live (9 probes: non-member 403 on create/list/revoke, replay 400, dup 409); EDGE CASES = probed empirically (unicode/300-char/whitespace names, negative/zero team ids, dup member, invalid email/role) and locked into 17 committed tests in tests/test_teams.py; ERROR HANDLING = all errors via HTTPException -> error_envelope by construction (M3 discipline), IntegrityError rollback on duplicates and one-time-use accept; NAMING = verb-first, router/service/schema split matched links.py in the convention check (M3); TEST COVERAGE = THE real gap found and closed -- team feature went from ZERO committed tests to 17, suite 75 -> 92 green. The phase shift matters: I stopped asking 'does it compile' and started asking 'what would a reviewer at 2AM find'. The honest weakness I tracked: my accept endpoint intentionally lets any authenticated user with the token accept (token = bearer of acceptance intent); replay is blocked atomically. Decision recap: review_method = hybrid (pattern-based first pass + targeted line-by-line on auth/mutation paths + empirical verification) -- and the empirical part is what caught the real issues (the redact bug in M3, the coverage gap in M4).
evidence: 5/5 edge tests + 17 committed tests in tests/test_teams.py
Review method: hybrid, with empirical verification as the deciding layer
